title: Paper Coffee Cups Release Millions of Nanoplastics
paragraphs: Millions of people around the world drink coffee from paper cups every day. However, a new study from Australia suggests that these cups may release millions of tiny plastic particles into hot drinks.

Although they are made mainly of paper, most disposable coffee cups have a thin plastic lining on the inside to stop liquid from leaking through. The study, carried out by researchers at the University of Queensland and led by Dr. Elvis Okoffo, examined two types of linings. One was made of polyethylene, a common plastic made from fossil fuels. The other was made of polylactic acid, or PLA, a so-called biodegradable plastic that is often used in cups marketed as more environmentally friendly. The study was published in the journal ACS Food Science & Technology in August 2026.

The researchers exposed the cups to hot liquid and then measured the plastic particles that were released. They found that both types of cups released large numbers of nanoplastics, which are particles about a thousand times thinner than a human hair. The cups lined with polyethylene released about 2.7 million particles per milliliter of liquid. Surprisingly, the cups with biodegradable PLA linings released even more, about 4.3 million particles per milliliter. In terms of total weight, the PLA-lined cups released about 12 times more plastic.

According to Okoffo, the study adds to growing evidence that plastic products used to store and prepare food are a significant but often overlooked way in which humans swallow plastic. However, the health effects of these particles are still unclear.

Okoffo stressed that the findings do not mean that people should stop using paper cups, or that PLA is necessarily unsafe. Instead, the researchers believe consumers should be told what materials are used to line paper cups. They also suggest that regulators should consider whether testing for particle release should be part of food safety checks, especially for products used with hot drinks. Meanwhile, manufacturers could develop linings that release fewer particles.

An earlier study by researchers at the same university, published in January 2026, found that cups made entirely of plastic released more microplastics than paper cups with plastic linings. It also found that hot water increased the release of microplastics from plastic cups by about a third.
